opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that both are unresolved, but they're unresolved in very different ways, and people often conflate them.

On the hardware side, a lot of the core problems are actually tractable engineering problems. We know what good looks like: actuators that are strong but backdrivable, hands that are robust enough to survive real contact, tactile sensing that doesn't fall apart after a few thousand cycles, and all of it at a cost that makes deployment at scale realistic. None of these are solved, especially hands and touch. Those are still the weakest link in most systems. But the path forward is relatively clear. It's iteration, supply chain, manufacturing, reliability testing. It's hard and slow, but it's the kind of hard where you can see the mountain you're climbing.

Software, and by that I mean intelligence, the policy that actually decides what the robot does, is unresolved in a deeper sense. We don't yet have a clear recipe for getting general, robust manipulation. We have promising directions: large-scale imitation learning, vision-language-action models, reinforcement learning on top of pretrained policies, simulation. But nobody can tell you with confidence what the scaling law is, what kind of data matters most, or how much is enough. That uncertainty is qualitatively different from "we need a better motor."

So if you ask me which is the bottleneck, I'd say today it's mostly the intelligence. A skilled human teleoperating even a fairly cheap, imperfect robot arm can do a surprising range of tasks: fold laundry, cook, tidy up. That tells you the hardware is already capable of much more than our autonomous policies can extract from it. The gap between what the hardware can do under human control and what it does on its own is basically the size of the software problem.

That said, I don't think you can fully separate them. Hardware shapes what data you can collect and how cheaply. If your robot breaks every few hours, you can't run large-scale data collection or real-world RL. If your hand has no sense of touch, your policy is learning with one eye closed. So in practice, the best progress comes from co-designing the two: building hardware that's good enough, cheap enough, and robust enough to feed the learning flywheel, and then letting the data and models drive what you improve next on the hardware.

If I had to summarize: hardware is a hard problem we roughly know how to solve; intelligence is a hard problem we're still figuring out how to frame. And the interesting work is at the interface between them.

r001.rationale: It describes hardware performing a wide range of tasks under human control while autonomous policies fail to extract that capability, identifying the gap as the software problem.

r002.rationale: It advocates co-designing hardware and software, but does not propose inventing simple hardware specifically suited to existing algorithms.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I'd say the honest answer is that both are unresolved, but they're unresolved in very different ways, and conflating them leads people to bad conclusions.

On the hardware side, I don't think the problem is that we can't build a good robot body. If you look at what's come out in the last few years, the actuators, the sensors, the hands, they're genuinely impressive. The problem is cost, reliability, and consistency at scale. A humanoid that works beautifully in a demo but needs a technician every two hundred hours isn't a product. And a hand that costs as much as a car doesn't get deployed in a warehouse. So hardware is an engineering and manufacturing problem more than a science problem. Those get solved, but they get solved slowly, through volume and iteration. It's the kind of thing where you need to ship ten thousand units to learn what breaks.

Software is the opposite. Software is where the real scientific uncertainty is. We still don't have a model that can walk into a kitchen it's never seen and reliably do something useful. We've made a lot of progress with large pretrained models and imitation learning, and the demos look great, but if you look closely, the generalization is still thin. Change the lighting, move the table a few centimeters, give it an object with a slightly different shape, and performance drops in ways that would be unacceptable for any real customer. The core question, how do you get robust, general manipulation from a reasonable amount of data, is not answered.

So if you ask me where the bottleneck is, I'd say software is the bottleneck for capability, and hardware is the bottleneck for deployment. And the uncomfortable part is that they're coupled. You can't collect the data to train the software without putting hardware in the world, and nobody wants to put hardware in the world until the software is good enough to be useful. Breaking that loop is really the whole game right now.

My own bias is that too many people are treating this like a pure AI problem, assuming the body is a solved commodity and all the value is in the model. I don't think that's right. The teams that win will be the ones that are willing to do the boring, unglamorous hardware work in parallel, because that's where your data actually comes from.

r001.rationale: It says robots still lack reliable, general manipulation in unfamiliar settings, emphasizing useful task performance and robustness as the core software question.

r002.rationale: It discusses improving and scaling hardware, but does not raise inventing simple hardware specifically suited to existing algorithms.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re deeply connected. Hardware sets the limits of what a robot can physically do—how precisely it can move, how much it can carry, how long it can operate, and what it costs. Software determines how well it uses those capabilities, especially when something unexpected happens.

If you’re doing a repetitive task in a controlled environment, the hardware may already be sufficient, and reliability or integration becomes the bigger challenge. If you want a robot to work in an unfamiliar home, you’re asking much more of perception, planning, and learning. But you also need hardware that can safely handle the physical variety of that environment.

So I wouldn’t assign a fixed percentage to each. I’d start with the task and ask: What’s preventing this robot from being useful? Sometimes it’s intelligence; sometimes it’s a gripper that can’t reliably pick something up. Progress comes from solving those together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses software using hardware capabilities and handling unexpected situations, but it does not identify the gap between movement and meaningful task performance as the central software challenge.

r002.rationale: It discusses hardware limits and solving hardware and software together, but does not raise inventing simple hardware suited to existing algorithms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both are still unresolved, but in different ways. Hardware sets the limits of what a robot can physically do: how much it can lift, how precisely it can move, how long it can operate, and how much it costs. Software determines how much of that capability we can actually use, especially when the environment changes or something unexpected happens.

The balance depends on the application. In a structured factory setting, you can get quite far with existing hardware and carefully engineered software. In a home, where objects, people, and tasks vary constantly, both become much harder. Better reasoning alone won’t compensate for a hand that can’t reliably grasp an object, and a very capable hand still needs software that knows what to do with it.

So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing which problem matters more. The important question is where the bottleneck is for a particular task, and whether improving one side actually improves the whole system.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes physical movement capability from software’s ability to use that capability, especially to handle changing environments and unexpected events, framing that gap as a software challenge.

r002.rationale: It discusses hardware limits and software needs, but does not propose inventing simple hardware tailored to existing algorithms.
